clue.text: Fell, given minute to get straight

parts.note: to align things is to put them in a straight line

explanation.surface: Someone knocked down is given a minute to stand up straight again, as in a boxing count.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fell' looks like a verb (knocked down) or a hill, but here it is the old adjective meaning cruel or deadly.
explanation.definitionFit: Fell as an adjective means fierce or evil, a synonym of the adjective malign.

clue.text: He sits down with one to pick team, say, from various possibilities

indicators.note: to pick here means to choose one result, signalling that the clue is describing what the answer's halves produce
from various possibilities says the word for a team is only one of several orderings a jumble could give

parts.note: the answer split in two reads as an instruction to jumble a word for friend, which produces this word as one example among the various possible orderings

explanation.surface: A captain sits down beside someone to choose a team from the available options.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads as an instruction: 'mess' the four-letter word for a friend and you get team, one of its various rearrangements. 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A messmate is a companion who eats at the same mess table, especially on board ship.

clue.text: Sort of officer is a strangely celebrated person outside

indicators.note: outside means the first piece is placed around the second

parts.note: a lion is a celebrity, as in a literary lion

indicators.note: strangely signals the two short words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A famous figure is somehow standing outside a particular kind of officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strangely' makes AIS from IS A, and 'outside' wraps it. A literary lion is a feted celebrity, a usage solvers outside Britain may not know.
explanation.definitionFit: A liaison officer coordinates between units or organisations.

clue.text: Sea lion, for example, that was in care of Chancellor

definitions.meaning: a large seal, taken literally as a big example of the animal

definitions.text: that was in care of Chancellor
definitions.meaning: the state seal of the realm, traditionally kept by the Lord Chancellor

explanation.walkthrough: The Lord Chancellor is a senior British officer of state who historically held the sovereign's seal.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names both a large seal animal, playfully, and the official seal of state held by the Lord Chancellor.

clue.text: Wasting gift, poet wanted to quibble

indicators.note: wasting suggests the words being squandered and broken down, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A poet, careless with his talent, ends up nitpicking over trifles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wasting' shuffles the eight letters of GIFT and POET; 'wanted to' is linking padding leading to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To pettifog is to argue over petty details, which is exactly what quibbling means.

clue.text: Love band in arena

parts.note: a band given as a pledge of love, and also a fight taking place in a boxing arena

explanation.definitionFit: The ring is a band given as a love token at betrothal; read another way it is a bout in a boxing ring.

clue.text: Having suppressed conflict, officer getting up to go fishing

indicators.note: in a down clue getting up means the whole assembly is read upwards, from bottom to top
having suppressed means the officer holds the conflict inside him

parts.note: LT is the abbreviation for lieutenant
war is a conflict

explanation.surface: An officer, having put down a war, heads off for some fishing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having suppressed' gives LWART, and 'getting up' turns it, as the light runs downwards. LT is the usual abbreviation for lieutenant.
explanation.definitionFit: To trawl is to fish by dragging a large net behind a boat.

clue.text: Attention in class: where is the radius?

indicators.note: in means the first piece sits inside the second

parts.note: a form is a school class
to give ear is to pay attention

explanation.surface: A teacher demands attention in a geometry class while asking where the radius is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is the container signal. The radius here is a bone, not a circle's measure, and a form is a British school class.
explanation.definitionFit: The radius is one of the two long bones of the lower arm, so the forearm is where it is found.

clue.text: Very eager colt's attempt to catch horse

parts.note: a Colt is a make of revolver, so a gun

indicators.note: to catch means the attempt encloses the next piece

parts.note: a go is an attempt
H is slang for heroin, which is also called horse

explanation.surface: A young horse makes an attempt to catch an older horse.
explanation.walkthrough: Colt looks like a young horse, but is the revolver. 'to catch' puts H inside GO.
explanation.definitionFit: Gung-ho describes someone enthusiastically, even recklessly, eager.

clue.text: Old translator's long-distance call, not all across valley

parts.note: a long distance is many miles

indicators.note: not means the following word is taken away from the one before

parts.note: over can mean across, as in over the road
a dale is a valley

explanation.surface: An old translator's long-distance phone call is cut off partway across a valley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not all' removes ALL from CALL to leave C. Miles Coverdale produced the first complete printed English Bible in 1535.
explanation.definitionFit: Miles Coverdale was a 16th-century English cleric who translated the Bible into English.

clue.text: Circle of people bound to be desperately anxious

indicators.note: of here puts the circle phrase after the description of its members, so the people come first in the answer

parts.note: slaves are people bound in servitude
a ring is a circle

explanation.surface: A group of shackled captives is understandably full of dread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' sets the order, people before circle. Bound looks like the end of a journey or a leap, but means shackled.
explanation.definitionFit: Slavering literally means drooling, and by extension being greedily or desperately eager for something.

clue.text: Space in front of curtain area likely to be short

definitions.meaning: the part of a theatre stage projecting forward of the proscenium curtain
on a golf course, the closely mown fringe around the green where the grass is kept short

explanation.surface: A theatre manager notes that the strip before the curtain is probably too small.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' looks like it means too small, but refers to closely cut grass on a golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the forestage of a theatre and the mown margin round a golf green carry this name.

clue.text: Bagpipe collection one's silent about

indicators.note: about means the first word goes around the second, enclosing it

parts.note: someone who is silent is mute
a set is a collection

explanation.surface: A set of bagpipes surrounds a player who is keeping very quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' makes the silent one surround the collection. 'one's silent' looks like a statement about the bagpipe player but is just the adjective made into a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A musette is a small French bagpipe popular in the 17th and 18th centuries.

clue.text: Giant pig grabbing dog's back

indicators.note: back tells us to read the whole assembled string from right to left
grabbing means the pig holds the dog inside it

parts.note: a hog is a pig
to dog someone is to follow them closely, to tail them

explanation.surface: A huge pig seizes a dog by its hindquarters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grabbing' gives HTAILOG; 'back' then reverses all of it. 'dog's back' tempts you to take the last letter of dog; the verb sense, to follow, is what is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Goliath, the Philistine champion slain by David, is the byword for a giant.

clue.text: Good body condition involves new weight

indicators.note: involves means the first piece takes the second inside it

parts.note: muscle tone is the firmness of a fit body

explanation.surface: Getting in shape means taking on a new weight-training regime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involves' puts N inside TONE.
explanation.definitionFit: A tonne is a metric unit of weight equal to 1,000 kilograms.

clue.text: Make more than one approach — that's not good enough

indicators.note: more than one approach means the word is given twice

parts.note: to come is to approach

explanation.surface: Someone making repeated advances is told that they fall short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make' is a link word. The phrase is a mild rebuke said when someone has not done enough.
explanation.definitionFit: The doubled exclamation is a mild reproof, a way of telling someone their effort or excuse falls short.

clue.text: Partner's fit to take on dog I abandoned

indicators.note: to take on means the fit is added on after the dog
abandoned means the letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: a collie is a breed of dog
an ague is a fit of fever and shivering

explanation.surface: A partner is fit enough to take on a dog that the owner gave up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abandoned' leaves COLLE; 'to take on' puts the fit after it. 'Partner's' reads as 'partner is', so the 's is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A colleague is a fellow worker, a partner in one's job or profession.

clue.text: Start to freeze hard with ice

indicators.note: start to means only the opening letter of the next word is taken

parts.note: hard as an adverb, meaning stiffly, is rigidly

explanation.surface: Water begins to freeze solid, turning into ice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hard' looks like an adjective but is the adverb RIGIDLY. 'with ice' means coldly in manner.
explanation.definitionFit: To act with ice is to act coldly, with no warmth, which is what frigidly means.

clue.text: What Stainer does, we hear, to take leading position as composer

indicators.note: we hear tells us the word is to be taken by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: someone who stains things sullies them
the van, short for vanguard, is the leading position

explanation.surface: The Victorian composer John Stainer takes the top spot among composers.
explanation.walkthrough: Stainer looks like the Victorian composer John Stainer, but here it is just someone who stains. Arthur Sullivan wrote the operettas with Gilbert.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Arthur Sullivan was a Victorian composer, best known for the Gilbert and Sullivan comic operas.

clue.text: Not changing college application document

parts.note: uni is short for university, a college
a form is the document filled in for an application

explanation.surface: A college applicant's document stays the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Uniform as an adjective means unvarying, remaining the same throughout.

clue.text: Cow inferior

definitions.meaning: something that lows, or moos, which is what a cow does

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cow' is not a verb meaning intimidate; it is the animal, as one that lows.
explanation.definitionFit: A cow is literally one that lows, and lower also means below in rank or quality.

clue.text: For something, ask in vain —- blow it!

definitions.meaning: to ask for something with no hope of getting it, idiomatically said with the word 'for' after
to blow is to sound a high note through pursed lips or an instrument

explanation.walkthrough: 'blow it!' looks like an exclamation of annoyance, but means blow (a referee's instrument or one's lips).
explanation.definitionFit: You can whistle for something you will never get, and to whistle is also to blow.

clue.text: Finish with charge in court

parts.note: a rap is a criminal charge, as in a murder rap
up means appearing before a court, as in up before the magistrate

explanation.surface: A trial ends with a charge laid in court.
explanation.definitionFit: To wrap up is to bring something to a finish or conclusion.

clue.text: I interrupted lodger, having to change last bed

indicators.note: interrupted means the letter breaks into the middle of the other word

parts.note: a lodger who pays rent is a renter

explanation.surface: A landlord barges in on a tenant who needs to move to a new bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'interrupted' puts I inside RENTER. 'last bed' is a grave, so changing it means burying again.
explanation.definitionFit: To reinter is to bury a body again, moving it to a new final resting place.

clue.text: Tick in box for title role

indicators.note: in means the first piece sits inside the second

parts.note: a tin is a box
a tick is a moment, informally a mo

explanation.surface: Mark a tick in a box to choose who plays the leading part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tick' suggests a check mark, but means a moment. Timon is the title character of Shakespeare's Timon of Athens.
explanation.definitionFit: Timon is the title role in Shakespeare's play Timon of Athens.

clue.text: Showing effect of shock, as circuit is broken by something electric

indicators.note: is broken by means the first piece is split open by the second

parts.note: a ring is a circuit
an electric eel can deliver an electric shock

explanation.surface: Someone is stunned when an electrical circuit is interrupted by a live component.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is broken by' is the container signal. The electric surface points to wiring; the something electric is in fact a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Reeling means staggering or stunned, as someone is after a shock.

clue.text: Albert Hall event includes a mixed type of competition

indicators.note: includes means the first piece holds the second inside it

parts.note: the Proms are a summer series of concerts at the Royal Albert Hall in London

explanation.surface: A concert at the Royal Albert Hall features a mixed contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'includes' puts A inside PROM.
explanation.definitionFit: A pro-am is a contest, often golf, in which professionals and amateurs play together.

clue.text: Began to reform a delinquent, but gave up

indicators.note: to reform is to remake, so the letters of the word are rebuilt in a new order

parts.note: a Ted, or Teddy boy, was a 1950s British youth associated with delinquency

explanation.surface: A social worker set out to straighten out a young offender, but then quit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to reform' makes ABNEG. Ted, short for Teddy boy, was a 1950s British youth in Edwardian-style clothes, seen as a delinquent. 'but' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To abnegate is to renounce or give up something, such as a right or a pleasure.

clue.text: Housing parent, consider protection against infection

indicators.note: housing means the first piece contains the second

parts.note: to ponder is to consider
Ma is an informal word for mother

explanation.surface: Someone looking after a parent weighs up how to guard against disease.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Housing' is the container signal. Pomanders, scented balls, were carried to ward off disease in the days of plague.
explanation.definitionFit: A pomander was a ball of aromatic substances carried in the belief it protected against plague and infection.

clue.text: Expedition dropped it as food

indicators.note: dropped means a piece is taken out of the longer word

parts.note: expedition in the sense of speed or promptness is celerity

explanation.surface: An expedition team ditched something because it was edible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expedition' suggests a journey, but here it means speed. 'as' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Celery is a vegetable eaten raw or cooked, so it counts as a food.
